newsitem.title: USA: U.S., China hail ties; agree on port calls.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China hail ties; agree on port calls.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen on Monday hailed positive momentum in bilateral ties, but their two-hour meeting produced little immediate achievement beyond an agreement on navy port calls to Hong Kong.

Despite upbeat comments about China's bid to join the World Trade Organization and the much-improved trend in Sino-American relations, Albright again pressed Beijing for "concrete and meaningful steps" in major areas of contention where there had been little or no movement, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

These included human rights, arms-related export controls and the importance of preserving autonomy and basic freedoms in Hong Kong when the British colony reverts to China's control on July 1, he said.

Separately, Chinese spokesman Shen Guofang told reporters that despite U.S. suspicions raised by Albright, China "has no nuclear cooperation with Iran whatsoever" and "has never been engaged in any activities like political donations" to U.S. election campaigns, as recent media reports have alleged.
On human rights, Shen said "the U.S. side (told Qian) it would not seek confrontation (while) the Chinese side said it would discuss human rights issues on the basis of equality."

The two ministers, who last met in February in Beijing, held a working dinner after their meeting. They are preparing the way for a fall summit in Washington between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.

Although Albright and Burns insisted the summit was on target for the fall, no specific date has been announced, raising suspicions the U.S. side is waiting to see what happens when Hong Kong changes hands.
Burns said during their "good and constructive meeting," the two ministers gave final approval to an agreement setting terms for U.S. Navy port calls in Hong Kong after July 1.
In December, U.S. and Chinese defense ministers agreed in principle that port calls would continue, but now there is a specific understanding on procedures for those visits, Burns said.

Monday's meeting began on a positive note, with Albright telling reporters "for both America and China, the benefits of our dialogue are tangible and growing. We're not yet where we want to be but the direction in which we must go is clear."
With the planned exchange of summits this year and next, "this is a pivotal year for U.S.-China relations," she said.

Qian was also upbeat, saying "through the concerted efforts of both sides, Sino-U.S. relations have maintained the positive momentum of improvement and development" begun late last year after a long period of dangerous deterioration.
"Although there are some differences between China and the United States, they are far outnumbered by our common views."
Albright and Qian were optimistic about prospects for an agreement this year on China's joining the WTO. Demands that China improve market access have delayed Beijing's entry.
Later, Burns tempered expectations an accord could be done by the summit, saying "I'm not sure when it can get done."

He said Albright stressed China's need to open its markets further to American goods and reduce the U.S.-China trade deficit. Shen said Qian told Albright that China would continue to expand its markets, especially in the purchase of U.S. aircraft and other high-tech items.
The most time was spent on non-proliferation, an issue on which Albright said Chinese efforts were uneven, Burns said.

He said "she noted that we've made little progress in areas that are or great concern to the United States -- (alleged) chemical and missile-related transfers to Iran and Pakistan ... and that we want to further our cooperation."

Shen said: "Qian said China has never engaged in the proliferation of nuclear weapons or technology. China has no nuclear cooperation with Iran whatsoever ... China will continue to improve its regulations and restrictions in this regard."

Recent media reports that top Chinese officials may have approved attempts to influence U.S. elections through 1996 campaign donations have caused a furor and clouded the debate over renewing China's Most Favored Nation trade status.
Qian reiterated Beijing's contention that it had no role in the alleged political contribution scandal, saying: "They (the charges) have nothing to do with China."
Qian was to meet Defense Secretary William Cohen on Tuesday and Clinton on Wednesday.
